name: LM27313XMFX_NOPB
title: 1.6 MHz current-mode boost converter, 30 V internal switch, SOT-23

source.revision: SNVS487E, December 2006, revised January 2015 (addendum pages dated 2025)

summary: The LM27313 is a step-up regulator in a five-pin SOT-23 that switches an internal 30 V DMOS transistor at a fixed 1.6 MHz under peak-current-mode control, with the loop compensated on chip. It runs from 2.7 V to 14 V in, is aimed at outputs of roughly 5 V to 28 V, and the switch limits at 0.8 A minimum cycle by cycle. An active-low SHDN input drops the supply current to tens of nanoamps, and thermal shutdown is built in. LM27313-Q1 is the AEC-Q100 Grade 1 version.
key_figures: 500 mΩ typ, 650 mΩ max at 100 mA
1.6 MHz typ, 1.15 to 1.90 MHz over temperature

pins.name: SW
pins.function: Switch node: the drain of the internal DMOS transistor. Wire it to the inductor and the anode of the rectifier.

pins.name: GND
pins.function: Ground for both the control circuitry and the switch current.

pins.name: FB
pins.function: Feedback input, regulated to 1.23 V; it takes the tap of the divider from the output that sets VOUT.

pins.name: SHDN
pins.function: Active-low shutdown. High runs the converter, low turns it off; tie it to VIN when shutdown is not wanted, and never leave it open.

pins.name: VIN
pins.function: Supply for the control circuitry and the switch driver, 2.7 V to 14 V.

circuits.title: 5 V to 12 V boost (Figure 12)
circuits.description: A 12 V boost from a 5 V supply. L1 stores energy while the internal switch pulls SW low and dumps it through Schottky D1 into C2 when the switch opens. R1 over R2 sets the output against the 1.23 V feedback reference; CF across R1 adds the loop zero the part needs for stability. R3 holds SHDN high from the input so the converter runs unless SHDN is pulled low. C1 is the ceramic input reservoir. Typical output capability 260 mA.
notes: Design load 250 mA; 260 mA typical output.

R3 holds SHDN high from the input so the converter runs unless SHDN is pulled low. C1 is the ceramic input reservoir. Typical output capability 130 mA.

operation.text: The converter runs at a fixed 1.6 MHz with peak-current-mode control. Each clock sets a latch that turns the DMOS switch on. A 50 mΩ resistor in the switch source turns the switch current into a voltage; this, plus the ramp from a ramp generator, is compared with the output of a transconductance error amplifier, and when it crosses, the latch resets and the switch turns off. An internal bandgap built around Q1 and Q2 sets the regulation point at FB, so the peak current each cycle is whatever holds FB at 1.23 V. The compensation network (RC, CC in the block diagram) is inside the part.

A separate comparator watches the same sense voltage and resets the latch directly when the switch current hits the limit, ending that cycle whatever the PWM comparator says; the switch stays off until the next clock. The limit is at least 0.8 A for duty cycles up to 50 % and falls at higher duty cycles (Figure 15).
An internal thermal shutdown circuit also resets the latch, turning the switch off.

Internally: VIN feeds a bandgap made of Q1 and Q2 (Q2 ten times Q1's area) with resistors R3 30 kΩ, R4 140 kΩ, R5 and R6; FB drives Q1's base. The Gm amplifier's output, filtered by RC and CC to ground, goes to the PWM comparator, whose other input is the sum of the sensed current and the ramp from the ramp generator; the oscillator drives the latch's set input. The PWM comparator, the current limit comparator and thermal shutdown each reset the latch, whose output reaches the switch gate through a driver stage; the shutdown circuitry is fed from pin 4. The switch drain is pin 1 and its 0.05 Ω sense resistor returns to pin 2.

Driving SHDN above 1.5 V runs the converter; below 0.50 V it is off, drawing 24 nA typical and 1 µA at most. The pin must not float: tie it straight to VIN if unused, or, to use shutdown, pull it up to VIN through 50 kΩ to 100 kΩ (the typical circuits use 51 kΩ) or drive it actively high and low. Its voltage must stay between 0 V and VIN.

The supply must stay above 2.7 V (and at most 14 V) while delivering the peak input current. When the source is more than a few inches from the IC, bulk capacitance may be needed beside the ceramic input capacitors.

The switch gate is driven from VIN and clamped internally at 5 V, so on-resistance is flat above VIN = 5 V and rises at lower inputs (Figure 7, about 0.44 Ω above 6 V and 0.57 Ω near 2.7 V). For the design equations, VSW can be estimated as RDS(ON) multiplied by IIND(AVG).

Use a ceramic capacitor, 2.2 µF nominal or larger; it supplies the inductor's current pulse each time the switch closes, so its ESR and ESL must be very low. It also keeps switching ripple off the input line.

One ceramic capacitor of 4.7 µF to 10 µF suits most designs; below 10 V out use 10 µF. Tantalum parts may be added in parallel for line support and transient response. Ordinary aluminium electrolytics are not suited above 500 kHz because of ringing and self-heating; ultra-low-ESR aluminium types (Sanyo Oscon) work but are costly. Too much ESR on the output erodes phase margin and can cause instability.

Only X5R or X7R ceramics should be used. Other dielectrics (Z5U, Y5F) can lose so much capacitance with temperature and bias that as little as 20 % of the rated value remains. Electrolytics resonate below the 1.6 MHz switching frequency and cannot supply the switching current alone, though they may sit beside the ceramics as bulk storage. Ceramic sources named: Taiyo-Yuden, AVX, Murata.

Even with internal compensation, CF across R1 is required: without the zero it adds, the loop can oscillate. Place the zero near 8 kHz (Cf = 1 / (2π R1 fz)); the typical circuits use 220 pF with 117 kΩ and 120 pF with 205 kΩ.

Use a Schottky. For switch voltages below 15 V a 20 V part (MBR0520); 15 V to 25 V a 30 V part (MBR0530); above 25 V a 40 V part (MBR0540). The MBR05xx parts carry 500 mA average; for loads up to 800 mA a UPS5817 is named.
R2 from FB to ground is suggested at 13.3 kΩ (about 92 µA of divider current) and R1 from the output to FB follows from R1 = R2 × (VOUT / VFB - 1).

The maximum duty cycle (88 % typical, 80 % minimum) caps how far VOUT can exceed VIN in continuous conduction. Losses in the inductor, switch, diode and capacitors push the measured duty cycle a little above the ideal formula; 1 - efficiency × VIN / VOUT is the better estimate, and it is the quantity used on the x axis of Figure 15.

Because the switch current is limited at its peak, a larger inductor lowers ripple and lets more of that peak go to the load, and keeps the converter in continuous conduction over a wider load range, improving load regulation and lowering output ripple. In the 5 V to 12 V example with 10 µH the on-time is 0.390 µs, the ripple is 0.176 A peak to peak, and the converter becomes discontinuous below about 33 mA of load (Figure 14).

Where load is small the inductor can be shrunk and the converter allowed to run discontinuously, provided the current never reaches the 800 mA limit within the longest possible on-time. That on-time is set by the slowest clock (1.15 MHz, 0.870 µs period) times the duty cycle. For 5 V to 12 V with 4.8 V across the inductor and 0.524 µs on-time the minimum is 3.144 µH, so 3.3 µH works if it holds its inductance up to 800 mA (Figure 17).

Pick a part that does not saturate at the peak current on its continuous rating, with a core type that keeps core (switching) loss low, and account for winding loss in the current rating. Suppliers named: Sumida, Coilcraft, Panasonic, TDK, Murata. Size the inductor for the full load plus the peaks seen at start-up and during load steps; start-up inrush depends on the output capacitance.
Figure 16 gives measured maximum load current for a typical device at 15 V, 20 V and 25 V out against input voltage; the ILOAD(max) expression gives a calculated estimate.
With SHDN tied to VIN through 51 kΩ and the 5 V to 12 V circuit, the output reaches 12 V about 1 ms after the input is applied at VIN = 3.3 V and about 0.6 ms after at VIN = 5 V (Figures 18 and 19).

At high duty cycles the longer on-time makes dissipation in the switch, rather than the current limit, set the maximum output current. Its conduction loss is DC × IIND(AVG)² × RDS(ON); switching losses come on top, so derate. RθJA is 166.3 °C/W in the DBV package.

Keep every part close to the IC; a four-layer board with inner ground planes is preferred. Keep the path between L1, D1 and C2 very short: trace inductance in series with D1 and C2 adds noise and ringing. FB is high impedance: keep R1, R2 and CF close to pin 3. With an inner ground plane, drop vias straight to it at pin 2 and at the ground ends of C1 and C2.

Suggested placement (Figure 22): U1 in the middle with C1 immediately beside it and L1 to its right over the VIN copper; D1 and C2 together above U1, D1 leading to the VOUT copper; R1, CF and R2 stacked down the left edge next to the FB side of U1; R3 below U1 on the shutdown trace. Pairs of ground vias sit at the ground pads of C2 and C1, and one at U1's ground pin.

LM27313-Q1 (part numbers LM27313XQ...) carries AEC-Q100 Grade 1 qualification covering -40 °C to 125 °C junction temperature; LM27313 is the catalog grade. Both share the electrical tables. Package markings: SRPB for LM27313, SD3B for LM27313-Q1.
ESD protection on the die is modest; store and handle it with the leads shorted or in conductive foam.
